findings.category: A03 Injection (CWE-78 OS Command Injection — local self-impact)
findings.title: icacls execSync uses string-interpolation, not argv array — quote-escape bypass possible if `path` or `user` contain double-quotes
findings.description: restrictFileMode builds the icacls command with template-literal interpolation: `icacls "${path}" /inheritance:r /grant:r "${user}:F"`. While both arguments are wrapped in double-quotes, neither is escaped. On Windows, if `path` contains a literal `"` (e.g. a user-supplied --file path like `C:\foo".bat`), the quote terminates the icacls argument and remaining bytes are interpreted as further shell tokens. `restrictFileMode` is callable via `runIdentityExport` (identity.ts:207) where `opts.file` is direct user CLI input. The same concern applies — much less plausibly — to `process.env.USERNAME`. Additionally the `path` for identity.json/token.json is derived from `homedir()` which on Windows could legitimately contain a space (handled by the quotes) but not a double-quote (rare but not impossible if a user has a maliciously-named profile dir).
findings.exploit_scenario: User runs `mnemonic identity export --file 'C:\Users\me\foo".bat" & calc.exe & x'`. On Windows, after writeFileSync succeeds, restrictFileMode would execSync `icacls "C:\Users\me\foo".bat" & calc.exe & x" /inheritance:r /grant:r "USER:F"` — the embedded quote terminates the first argument and `calc.exe` runs. Because the user typed the path themselves, this is local self-impact (the user attacks themselves), not a remote/network vulnerability.
findings.impact: Local self-impact only. No privilege escalation (icacls runs as the same user). Worst case: shell command injection via the user's own input. Not a credential-exfil vector unless wrapped by a higher-level tool that lets a remote actor smuggle the --file path.
findings.notes: Comment on line 72 claims 'Quote both arguments to defeat path/username spaces' — quoting handles spaces but not embedded quotes. Comment is misleading and should be corrected if the fix is not applied.

findings.title: Authorize URL printed to stderr on every interactive login — exposes state + code_challenge in scrollback
findings.description: `hint('opening browser: ${authz.url}', opts)` echoes the full authorize URL — including `state` (random nonce) and `code_challenge` (PKCE S256 derivative) — to stderr. Neither is a secret per RFC 7636 (state is a CSRF token; code_challenge is a one-way SHA-256 hash). However if a user pipes stderr to a shared log, an observer who also has access to the in-memory `verifier` could in principle replay; but verifier is never persisted, so this is moot.
findings.impact: None — `state` and `code_challenge` are not secrets. Listed for completeness only.
findings.recommendation: No action required. If desired, redact the query string from the printed URL: `hint('opening browser: ${baseUrl}/oauth/authorize?...', opts)` — but this hurts diagnosability when something goes wrong.

findings.title: Token expiry uses wall-clock (Date.now()) — no leeway for clock skew
findings.description: loadToken throws if `Date.parse(expires_at) <= Date.now()`. There is no clock-skew window. If the user's clock is fast, a not-yet-expired JWT could be rejected by the CLI even though the server still accepts it.
findings.impact: Low — at worst the user re-runs `mnemonic login`. Conservative direction (fail-closed).
findings.recommendation: No action required for security. SDK's parseJwtPayload uses the same strict comparison so behaviour is consistent.

findings.title: Loopback callback responder accepts any GET path (not just /callback) — but rejects with 404
findings.description: The HTTP server is bound only to 127.0.0.1, which RFC 8252 §7.3 explicitly endorses for native apps. A scanner on the loopback interface could probe the random port; the server replies 405 to non-GET and 404 to non-/callback paths and does not consume the single-shot. This is correct behaviour. No timing-side-channel in the path comparison.

owasp_top10_summary: No critical/high issues. One low-severity finding (F-1 icacls quote-escape) — local self-impact only, easily fixed by switching to execFileSync argv-array. State-validation-before-exchange, JWT alg whitelist, redaction pipeline, loopback hardening, and 0600 file modes are all correctly implemented and tested.

The core security invariants requested by Decision 5 (loopback 127.0.0.1, state-before-exchange, single-shot, 5-min timeout) and Decision 8 (0600 / icacls ACL) are all implemented and tested. The TDD anchor `interactive_loopback_state_validation` is present and passing. F-1 should be addressed before publish but does not block T5 completion.
